title: What's the deal with Swiss neutrality?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Swiss neutrality, tracing its roots from the 1291 Everlasting Alliance of Alpine cantons through the sixteenth-century decline of Swiss mercenary power after the 1515 Battle of Marignano, the 1648 Peace of Westphalia recognition, the Napoleonic era and the 1815 Congress of Vienna, to the 1907 Hague Convention rules and World War II. They cover Switzerland's role as an arbitration and mediation host (Alabama Claims, good offices, representing states that don't talk to each other), the Red Cross origins with Henry Dunant and the first Geneva Convention, the secret Swiss banking system and its decline, Nazi gold and dormant Holocaust victim accounts, and the country's decisions to join the UN in 2002 and its refusal to join the EU or NATO. The episode ends with listener mail about M*A*S*H.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Swiss neutrality
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic, prompted by recent US-Iran talks in which Switzerland had a role, and joke about Switzerland's known attributes. They note other countries are neutral too.

segments.title: 1291 alliance and early Swiss confederation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Swiss Confederation of cantons, the 1291 alliance of three cantons, the free peasants of the Alps and their strategic mountain-pass location, and the legend of William Tell.

segments.title: Growth of the confederation and Swiss military reputation
segments.summary: The alliance grew with more cantons, and the Swiss became a feared fighting force in European wars, which Machiavelli called the new Romans.

segments.title: Battle of Marignano and turn toward neutrality
segments.summary: After losses at the Battle of Marignano in 1515, with about ten thousand infantry killed, the Swiss moved away from warring alliances. Religious divisions between Protestant and Catholic cantons, and a favorable financial deal with France, reinforced neutrality.

segments.title: Thirty Years War, Swiss army and Westphalia recognition
segments.summary: The Thirty Years War and religious divisions threatened neutrality. Cantons set troop quotas for a defense army in 1646. Johann Rudolf Wettstein, mayor of Basel, secured Swiss recognition as independent at the 1648 Peace of Westphalia.

segments.title: Napoleon, Helvetic Republic and Congress of Vienna
segments.summary: French revolutionary wars led to the French-created Helvetic Republic and Napoleon's occupation. Swiss troops suffered heavy losses in Russia in 1812. After Napoleon's defeat, Charles Pictet de Rochemont helped establish perpetual neutrality at the 1814/1815 Congress of Vienna.

segments.title: Transition to modern Switzerland
segments.summary: Modern Switzerland is described as a sovereign, officially neutral confederation.

segments.title: Hague Convention rules, Swiss army and World War II
segments.summary: Neutral states must follow Hague Convention rules, such as not sending troops, weapons or money to warring parties. Switzerland keeps an army and a conscription system for men aged 18 to 34, with conscientious objector options. During World War II, Switzerland was surrounded by the Axis and deterred invasion with a large army. The Swiss army knife is noted.

segments.title: Switzerland as arbitration and mediation host
segments.summary: Geneva and Basel chambers of commerce began a system of arbitration, starting with the 1872 Alabama Claims negotiations between the US and Britain in Geneva. Switzerland's good offices represent states that do not talk to each other, and the hosts speculate about fees.

segments.title: Henry Dunant, Red Cross and first Geneva Convention
segments.summary: Henry Dunant witnessed the aftermath of the 1859 Battle of Solferino and devoted his life to humanitarian aid, founding the first national Red Cross society and pushing for the first Geneva Convention in 1864. He later went bankrupt, was rediscovered, and shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with hosts reflecting on Henry Dunant.

segments.title: Swiss banking secrecy and the Federal Banking Act of 1934
segments.summary: Switzerland built its banking center on neutrality and secrecy, attracting dictators, launderers and tax evaders. The Federal Banking Act of 1934 codified secret accounts, which were later scaled back in the 1990s after image damage.

segments.title: Nazi gold and Holocaust victims' dormant accounts
segments.summary: The Swiss National Bank bought about 440 million dollars in Nazi gold, later returning only about twelve percent under the 1946 Washington Agreement. Swiss banks kept deposits of Holocaust victims whose heirs lacked death certificates. A 1998 settlement with the World Jewish Congress followed.

segments.title: Switzerland and the UN, EU and NATO
segments.summary: Switzerland joined the UN in 2002 after a close referendum and became a non-permanent UN Security Council member in 2023. It has declined to join the EU, citing net contribution costs, direct democracy, its neutral brand, and immigration concerns. It also is not in NATO.

segments.title: Closing reflections on Swiss neutrality
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up by noting Switzerland's neutrality brand and say they hope the country stays distinct.

segments.title: Listener mail: M*A*S*H follow-up
segments.summary: A listener named Dave from Vancouver writes about M*A*S*H, its handling of homosexuality, and a trivia game. The hosts mention live show tickets in Vancouver.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address and the show's production credit.
